title: {{NAME}} and the Crown of Living Scales
moral: Real royalty is measured not by what you wear on your head, but by what you carry in your heart.

pages.content: The Sunken Palace had not been entered in five hundred years, not since the great brachiosaurus had curled around its towers and gone to sleep, her scales slowly thickening into living stone. She breathed still, faint and slow, and the palace walls breathed with her. {{NAME}} arrived at the palace gates at dawn, the sky above a wash of coral and pale gold, and found them already open. A trail of enormous three-toed prints pressed deep into the courtyard grass, fresh and glistening. Beside each print, a smaller mark: a tiny boot heel. Someone had come here before him. He tugged the gold trim of his cobalt tunic straight, took a breath that tasted of old stone and wild jasmine, and walked inside. The brachiosaurus shifted in her sleep above him, scales clicking gently, and a shower of golden pollen drifted down like slow, warm snow.

pages.content: Inside the great hall, {{NAME}} found Princess Soraya standing on a marble throne, her arms stretched wide, absolutely motionless, while a flock of small striped lizards explored every fold of her violet gown. She had a crown of twisted silver on her head, but she was holding something more interesting: a single brachiosaurus egg, pale blue and enormous, cradled in both arms like a sleeping baby. She caught sight of {{NAME}} and her eyes went wide, not with fear, but with relief so fierce it looked like joy. She whispered, as if the lizards might be alarmed by full volume, that the egg had rolled loose from the mother's nest, which wound around the eastern tower, and that she had been standing still for forty minutes because the lizards had mistaken her for a comfortable boulder. {{NAME}} pressed his lips together very hard to keep from laughing out loud. He did not quite succeed.

pages.content: Getting the egg back to the nest required a plan, a very good one, executed very quickly. Soraya could not move without scattering the lizards, and {{NAME}} could not carry the egg alone because it was the size of a large watermelon and twice as heavy. So {{NAME}} gathered a trail of fallen golden pollen, laid it carefully across the marble floor, and blew it gently toward the lizards. Their striped heads swivelled in unison. Their tiny nostrils flared. Then they abandoned Soraya in a single enthusiastic surge, following the pollen trail like a river. Soraya descended the throne in three swift, soundless steps, the egg held steady. Together they ran through corridor after corridor, up spiralling stairs, out onto the eastern parapet where the nest waited, enormous and warm, woven from branches and old tapestry silk. They lowered the egg inside. It rocked once, settled, and began, very gently, to hum.

pages.content: The humming grew. The great brachiosaurus opened one eye. It was the colour of deep amber, enormous as a cartwheel, and it regarded the two children with the slow, unhurried focus of a creature who had been sleeping for centuries and was not yet certain it was worth being awake. Then the egg hummed again, a tiny warm pulse, and something shifted in that vast amber eye. The brachiosaurus lifted her head, her scales chiming softly, and lowered it with agonising slowness until her chin rested on the parapet beside the nest. She exhaled. The breath was warm and smelled of old forests and something green and ancient. Soraya reached up and placed her silver crown on the very tip of the great dinosaur's snout. It looked, somehow, exactly right there. The brachiosaurus blinked once. {{NAME}} had the strong feeling he was watching two queens recognise each other.

pages.content: The sun slid below the palace walls and the sky turned the colour of plums and warm honey. The brachiosaurus settled back around her towers, her breathing deep and steady, the silver crown balanced between her nostrils like a gift she intended to keep. Soraya sat beside {{NAME}} on the parapet steps, and neither of them spoke for a while because some moments are too full for words. Below, the striped lizards had reassembled into a neat column and were marching, with great purpose, toward the palace kitchens. {{NAME}} leaned back against the warm stone and felt tiredness settle over him like a comfortable blanket. Soraya pointed out the first star appearing above the eastern tower. It winked, once, as if in agreement about something. {{NAME}}'s eyes grew heavy and slow. He was nearly asleep when the egg in the nest let out one long, clear hum, a different note than before, higher and brighter and full of something new. Rest now. By morning, something wonderful might have changed.
